2dfeaeec.title: Attention Is All You Need Authors: Ashish Vaswani, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, Jakob Uszkoreit, Llion Jones, Aidan N. Gomez, Lukasz Kaiser, Illia Polosukhin
2dfeaeec.author: Unknown Author
2dfeaeec.abstract: The dominant sequence transduction models are based on complex recurrent or convolutional neural networks that include an encoder and a decoder. The best performing models also connect the encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism. We propose a new simple network architecture, the Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely. Experiments on two machine translation tasks show these models to be superior in quality while being more parallelizable and requiring significantly less time to train. Our model achieves 28.4 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, improving over the existing best results, including ensembles, by over 2 BLEU. On the WMT 2014 English-to-French translation task, our model establishes a new single-model state-of-the-art BLEU score of 41.8 after training for 3.5 days on eight GPUs.

full_text_pages.text:
Attention Is All You Need
Authors: Ashish Vaswani, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, Jakob Uszkoreit, Llion Jones, Aidan N. Gomez, Lukasz Kaiser, Illia Polosukhin
ABSTRACT
The dominant sequence transduction models are based on complex recurrent or convolutional neural networks that include an encoder and
a decoder. The best performing models also connect the encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism. We propose a new simple
network architecture, the Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely.
Experiments on two machine translation tasks show these models to be superior in quality while being more parallelizable and requiring
significantly less time to train. Our model achieves 28.4 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, improving over the
existing best results, including ensembles, by over 2 BLEU. On the WMT 2014 English-to-French translation task, our model establishes a
new single-model state-of-the-art BLEU score of 41.8 after training for 3.5 days on eight GPUs.
1. Introduction & Motivation
Recurrent neural networks, long short-term memory (LSTM) and gated recurrent units (GRU) have been firmly established as state of the
art approaches in sequence transduction problems such as machine translation. Recurrent models factor computation along symbol
positions. This inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples, which becomes critical at longer sequence
lengths. In this work we propose the Transformer, a model architecture eschewing recurrence and instead relying entirely on self-attention
mechanisms to compute representations of its input and output without using sequence-aligned RNNs or convolution.
2. Background & Related Architectural Paradigms
The goal of reducing sequential computation forms the foundation of Extended Neural GPU, ByteNet and ConvS2S, which use
convolutional networks. In these models, the number of operations required to relate signals from two arbitrary positions grows with
distance: linearly for ConvS2S and logarithmically for ByteNet. In the Transformer, this is reduced to a constant number of operations O(1)
via multi-head self-attention.
Page 1

3. Model Architecture & Scaled Dot-Product Attention
The Transformer follows an encoder-decoder architecture using stacked self-attention and point-wise, fully connected layers. The encoder
is composed of N = 6 identical layers, each with multi-head self-attention followed by a position-wise feed-forward network with residual
connections and layer normalization: Output = LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)).
Scaled Dot-Product Attention is computed as: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax((Q * K^T) / sqrt(d_k)) * V, where queries and keys have
dimension d_k = 64, and values have dimension d_v = 64. Scaling by 1 / sqrt(d_k) counteracts large magnitude dot products that push the
softmax function into regions with dangerously small gradients.
3.1 Multi-Head Attention Dynamics
Instead of performing a single attention function with d_model-dimensional keys, values, and queries, we project the queries, keys, and
values h = 8 times with different, learned linear projections to d_k, d_k, and d_v dimensions respectively: MultiHead(Q,K,V) =
Concat(head_1, ..., head_h) * W^O. Multi-head attention allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation
subspaces at different positions.
Page 2

4. Experimental Results and Translation Benchmarks
On the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, the Transformer (Big) model achieves 28.4 BLEU, outperforming existing models
and ensembles by >2.0 BLEU with an efficiency of 2.3 x 10^19 FLOPs. On WMT 2014 English-to-French, our model establishes 41.8 BLEU
with training time of 3.5 days on 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs.
5. Critical Limitations and Quadratic Scaling Constraints
Despite empirical dominance, self-attention suffers from fundamental algorithmic boundaries. First, memory and computational complexity
scale quadratically O(n^2) with sequence length n. This severely bounds context windows on long texts and genomic sequences. Second,
lack of recurrence requires absolute or learned positional encodings, which exhibit poor out-of-distribution length generalization on unseen
token distances.
6. Open Questions & Future Research Trajectories
Research is critically needed to design sub-quadratic or linear attention mechanisms (such as state-space models and kernelized
projections) and to extend attention mechanics natively to non-textual modalities without token fragmentation.
Page 3

4af32c6d.title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
4af32c6d.author: Unknown Author
4af32c6d.abstract: An important paradigm of natural language processing consists of large-scale pre-training on general domain data and adaptation to particular tasks or domains. As we pre-train larger models, full fine-tuning, which retrains all model parameters, becomes less feasible. Using GPT-3 175B as an example - deploying independent instances of fine-tuned models, each with 175B parameters, is prohibitively expensive. We propose Low-Rank Adaptation, or LoRA, which freezes the pre-trained model weights and injects trainable rank decomposition matrices into each layer of the Transformer architecture, greatly reducing the number of trainable parameters for downstream tasks. Compared to fine-tuning GPT-3 175B with Adam, LoRA can reduce the number of trainable parameters by 10,000 times and the GPU memory requirement by 3 times. LoRA performs on-par or better than fine-tuning in model quality on RoBERTa, DeBERTa, GPT-2, and GPT-3, despite having fewer trainable parameters.

full_text_pages.text:
LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
Authors: Edward J. Hu, Yelong Shen, Phillip Wallis, Zeyuan Allen-Zhu, Yuanzhi Li, Shean Wang, Lu Wang, Weizhu Chen
ABSTRACT
An important paradigm of natural language processing consists of large-scale pre-training on general domain data and adaptation to
particular tasks or domains. As we pre-train larger models, full fine-tuning, which retrains all model parameters, becomes less feasible.
Using GPT-3 175B as an example - deploying independent instances of fine-tuned models, each with 175B parameters, is prohibitively
expensive. We propose Low-Rank Adaptation, or LoRA, which freezes the pre-trained model weights and injects trainable rank
decomposition matrices into each layer of the Transformer architecture, greatly reducing the number of trainable parameters for
downstream tasks. Compared to fine-tuning GPT-3 175B with Adam, LoRA can reduce the number of trainable parameters by 10,000 times
and the GPU memory requirement by 3 times. LoRA performs on-par or better than fine-tuning in model quality on RoBERTa, DeBERTa,
GPT-2, and GPT-3, despite having fewer trainable parameters.
1. Introduction & Storage Bottleneck in Scale
Modern NLP relies on pre-training foundational language models and adapting them to specialized downstream tasks. Conventional
adaptation updates all parameters (full fine-tuning). For massive architectures like GPT-3 (175 billion parameters), storing and serving
distinct checkpoints requires 350 GB of VRAM per fine-tuned instance, creating extreme operational deployment barriers. We draw on
intrinsic dimensionality theory, which asserts that over-parametrized neural models reside on a low intrinsic manifold during task adaptation.
2. Mathematical Formulation of Low-Rank Decomposition
For a pre-trained weight matrix W_0 in R^(d x k), we constrain its weight update Delta W by representing it through low-rank decomposition:
W = W_0 + Delta W = W_0 + (alpha / r) * (B * A), where B in R^(d x r), A in R^(r x k), with rank r << min(d, k). Matrix A is initialized from a
Gaussian distribution N(0, sigma^2) while B is initialized to zero, ensuring Delta W = 0 at the start of adaptation. The scaling factor alpha / r
stabilizes optimization across variable rank choices.
Page 1

3. Algorithmic Advantages & Zero Deployment Latency
LoRA provides three key engineering benefits:
1. Memory Efficiency: Optimizer states for frozen weights W_0 are omitted from memory, reducing VRAM footprint by up to 3x.
2. Modular Checkpoints: Adapter weights (matrices A and B) occupy mere megabytes (e.g., 20 MB vs 350 GB for GPT-3).
3. Zero Inference Latency: In production deployment, we directly merge weights via W_merged = W_0 + (alpha / r) * (B * A), recovering
identical inference latency with zero architectural branching overhead during single-task serving.
Page 2

4. Quantitative Benchmarks Across Language Models
On GLUE benchmarks using RoBERTa-large and DeBERTa-XXL, LoRA matches or exceeds full fine-tuning accuracy while updating only
0.08% of parameters. On GPT-3 175B, LoRA attains 73.4% on WikiSQL and 65.8 BLEU on E2E NLG, surpassing prefix tuning and series
adapters.
5. Limitations and Deployment Vulnerabilities
LoRA exhibits specific constraints: Multi-tenant serving of mixed tasks in a single batched inference call incurs computational overhead
because dynamically swapping weight matrices W = W_0 + B_i * A_i per batch element requires custom kernel dispatch. Additionally,
determining optimal rank r per projection layer (W_q, W_k, W_v, W_o) currently relies on empirical grid search.
6. Future Work: Adaptive Rank Search & Quantized LoRA
Open questions include automated layer-wise rank allocation, theoretical convergence bounds under non-convex objectives, and unifying
LoRA with aggressive 4-bit NormalFloat weight quantization (QLoRA).
Page 3

bbf078e6.title: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
bbf078e6.author: Unknown Author
bbf078e6.abstract: Transformers are slow and memory-hungry on long sequences, since the time and memory complexity of self-attention are quadratic in sequence length. Approximate attention methods have attempted to address this compute and memory bottleneck by trading off model quality to achieve speedup, but often fail to achieve real-wallclock speedup. We argue that a missing principle is making attention algorithms IO-aware?accounting for reads and writes between levels of GPU memory (such as High Bandwidth Memory HBM and fast on-chip SRAM). We propose FlashAttention, an IO-aware exact attention algorithm that uses tiling to reduce the number of memory reads/writes between GPU HBM and SRAM. We analyze the IO complexity of FlashAttention, proving that it requires fewer HBM accesses than standard attention. FlashAttention trains Transformers 2-4x faster than standard PyTorch attention, scales linearly in sequence length memory footprint, and enables training on sequences up to 64k tokens.

full_text_pages.text:
FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
Authors: Tri Dao, Daniel Y. Fu, Stefano Ermon, Atri Rudra, Christopher Ré
ABSTRACT
Transformers are slow and memory-hungry on long sequences, since the time and memory complexity of self-attention are quadratic in
sequence length. Approximate attention methods have attempted to address this compute and memory bottleneck by trading off model
quality to achieve speedup, but often fail to achieve real-wallclock speedup. We argue that a missing principle is making attention
algorithms IO-aware?accounting for reads and writes between levels of GPU memory (such as High Bandwidth Memory HBM and fast
on-chip SRAM). We propose FlashAttention, an IO-aware exact attention algorithm that uses tiling to reduce the number of memory
reads/writes between GPU HBM and SRAM. We analyze the IO complexity of FlashAttention, proving that it requires fewer HBM accesses
than standard attention. FlashAttention trains Transformers 2-4x faster than standard PyTorch attention, scales linearly in sequence length
memory footprint, and enables training on sequences up to 64k tokens.
1. Introduction & The IO Bottleneck Principle
Standard attention implementations in PyTorch materialize the full intermediate N x N attention matrix S = Q * K^T and attention probability
matrix P = softmax(S) in GPU High Bandwidth Memory (HBM). Modern GPUs (such as NVIDIA A100) are memory-bandwidth-bound rather
than compute-bound for attention: SRAM bandwidth is ~19 TB/s while HBM bandwidth is only ~1.5 TB/s. Materializing large N x N matrices
in slow HBM dominates execution time, leading to memory-bound latency.
2. Hardware Foundations: The GPU Memory Hierarchy
To accelerate attention, algorithms must minimize reads and writes between slow HBM (40-80 GB) and small, fast on-chip SRAM (192 KB
per Streaming Multiprocessor). Theoretical FLOP reductions that ignore memory IO (such as sparse or low-rank attention) often yield zero
practical wall-clock speedup due to memory transfer overhead.
Page 1

3. FlashAttention Algorithm: Tiling and Online Softmax
FlashAttention computes exact attention using two synergistic techniques:
1. Tiling: We partition inputs Q, K, V into blocks that fit within SRAM. We evaluate softmax iteratively across blocks using the online softmax
formulation, maintaining running normalization statistics (m_i, l_i) without materializing the full N x N matrix in HBM.
2. Recomputation: In the backward pass, rather than reading saved N x N attention matrices from slow HBM, FlashAttention recomputes
attention blocks directly in fast SRAM using stored forward normalization statistics. This converts slow memory IO into fast arithmetic
compute.
Page 2

4. IO Complexity & End-to-End Speedups
FlashAttention requires O(N^2 * d^2 / M) HBM accesses where M is SRAM capacity, compared to standard attention which requires
Theta(N * d + N^2) HBM accesses?a 4x to 9x reduction in HBM traffic. Empirically, FlashAttention trains BERT-large 2.4x faster, GPT-2 3x
faster, and solves the Long Range Arena Path-X 16k benchmark with 86.4% accuracy where standard attention runs out of memory.
5. Hardware Constraints & Algorithmic Limitations
FlashAttention kernels require low-level CUDA and warp-level primitives tuned for specific GPU microarchitectures (SRAM sizes, warp
shuffles). Execution on non-NVIDIA accelerators or CPU clusters requires ground-up kernel rewriting. Furthermore, for sequence lengths >
100k, IO-aware exact attention still scales as O(N^2) total operations.
6. Future Directions
Key frontiers include hardware-aware multi-query attention, extending IO awareness to structured state space models (Mamba), and
mixed-precision FP8 SRAM tiling kernels.
Page 3

1247e25d.title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understandin
1247e25d.author: Unknown Author
1247e25d.abstract: We introduce a new language representation model called BERT, which stands for Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers. Unlike recent language representation models, BERT is designed to pre-train deep bidirectional representations from unlabeled text by jointly conditioning on both left and right context in all layers. As a result, the pre-trained BERT model can be fine-tuned with just one additional output layer to create state-of-the-art models for a wide range of tasks, such as question answering and language inference, without substantial task-specific architecture modifications. BERT is conceptually simple and empirically powerful. It obtains new state-of-the-art results on eleven natural language processing tasks, including pushing the GLUE score to 80.5%, MultiNLI accuracy to 86.7%, and SQuAD v1.1 question answering Test F1 to 93.2, outperforming human performance by 2.0 points.

full_text_pages.text:
BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understandin
Authors: Jacob Devlin, Ming-Wei Chang, Kenton Lee, Kristina Toutanova (Google AI Language)
ABSTRACT
We introduce a new language representation model called BERT, which stands for Bidirectional Encoder Representations from
Transformers. Unlike recent language representation models, BERT is designed to pre-train deep bidirectional representations from
unlabeled text by jointly conditioning on both left and right context in all layers. As a result, the pre-trained BERT model can be fine-tuned
with just one additional output layer to create state-of-the-art models for a wide range of tasks, such as question answering and language
inference, without substantial task-specific architecture modifications. BERT is conceptually simple and empirically powerful. It obtains new
state-of-the-art results on eleven natural language processing tasks, including pushing the GLUE score to 80.5%, MultiNLI accuracy to
86.7%, and SQuAD v1.1 question answering Test F1 to 93.2, outperforming human performance by 2.0 points.
1. Introduction: Limitations of Unidirectional Representations
Language model pre-training has shown exceptional efficacy for downstream NLP. However, standard architectures (such as OpenAI GPT)
employ unidirectional autoregressive architectures, where every token can only attend to previous tokens in self-attention layers. Such
left-to-right constraints are severely sub-optimal for sentence-level understanding and token-level tasks like question answering (SQuAD),
where integrating bidirectional context from both left and right directions is crucial.
2. The Masked Language Model (MLM) Objective
To train deep bidirectional representations without allowing tokens to trivially attend to themselves across multi-layer Transformers, we
introduce the Masked Language Model (MLM) objective. We randomly mask 15% of all input tokens. Of the selected tokens, 80% are
replaced with a special [MASK] token, 10% are replaced with a random token, and 10% are kept unchanged. The model is trained to
reconstruct the original token IDs via cross-entropy loss.
Page 1

3. Next Sentence Prediction (NSP) & Architecture
BERT incorporates a binarized Next Sentence Prediction (NSP) task: pairs of sentences A and B are provided, and the model predicts
whether B is the actual subsequent sentence in the corpus (IsNext) or a random document (NotNext). BERT uses a multi-layer bidirectional
Transformer encoder. BERT-Base has L = 12 layers, H = 768 hidden dimension, A = 12 attention heads (110M parameters). BERT-Large
has L = 24 layers, H = 1024 hidden dimension, A = 16 attention heads (340M parameters).
3.1 Task-Specific Fine-Tuning Pipeline
Fine-tuning is straightforward: task-specific inputs are formatted with special classification tokens [CLS] and separator tokens [SEP]. For
classification, the final hidden state of [CLS] is fed into a minimal classification layer W in R^(K x H), fine-tuning all model parameters
end-to-end with low training cost.
Page 2

4. State-of-the-Art Empirical Results
BERT establishes state-of-the-art performance across 11 NLP tasks. On GLUE, BERT-Large attains 80.5% average score (+7.7% over
OpenAI GPT). On SQuAD v1.1, it reaches 93.2 F1, outperforming the human benchmark (91.2 F1). On MultiNLI, it records 86.7% accuracy.
5. Methodological Limitations & Inference Inefficiency
BERT has distinct structural limitations: First, because it is an encoder-only masked model, it cannot perform open-ended autoregressive
text generation. Second, pre-train / fine-tune discrepancy exists: the [MASK] token never appears during fine-tuning or inference. Third,
quadratic self-attention limits inputs to a maximum sequence length of 512 tokens.
6. Future Trajectories
Pivotal directions include sequence length scaling via sparse attention, pre-training objectives eliminating the [MASK] artificial token
discrepancy (e.g., ELECTRA), and causal decoder cross-attention unification.
Page 3

ba07ce7a.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
ba07ce7a.author: Unknown Author
ba07ce7a.abstract: Large pre-trained language models have been shown to store factual knowledge in their parameters, and achieve state-of-the-art results when fine-tuned on downstream NLP tasks. However, their ability to access and precisely manipulate knowledge is still limited, and they often hallucinate on knowledge-intensive tasks. Furthermore, updating their stored knowledge requires retraining the entire network. We propose Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models, which combine pre-trained parametric memory (a sequence-to-sequence Transformer) with non-parametric memory (a dense vector index of Wikipedia accessed via a Dense Passage Retriever). We compare two RAG formulations: RAG-Sequence, which uses the same retrieved passage for an entire sequence, and RAG-Token, which can access different passages per token. We evaluate our models on open-domain QA (Natural Questions, WebQuestions, CuratedTREC) and knowledge verification (FEVER), achieving new state-of-the-art results.

full_text_pages.text:
Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
Authors: Patrick Lewis, Ethan Perez, Aleksandara Piktus, Fabio Petroni, Vladimir Karpukhin, Naman Goyal, Heinrich Küttler, Mike Lewis, Scott Yi
ABSTRACT
Large pre-trained language models have been shown to store factual knowledge in their parameters, and achieve state-of-the-art results
when fine-tuned on downstream NLP tasks. However, their ability to access and precisely manipulate knowledge is still limited, and they
often hallucinate on knowledge-intensive tasks. Furthermore, updating their stored knowledge requires retraining the entire network. We
propose Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models, which combine pre-trained parametric memory (a sequence-to-sequence
Transformer) with non-parametric memory (a dense vector index of Wikipedia accessed via a Dense Passage Retriever). We compare two
RAG formulations: RAG-Sequence, which uses the same retrieved passage for an entire sequence, and RAG-Token, which can access
different passages per token. We evaluate our models on open-domain QA (Natural Questions, WebQuestions, CuratedTREC) and
knowledge verification (FEVER), achieving new state-of-the-art results.
1. Introduction: Parametric vs Non-Parametric Memory
Pre-trained language models store substantial world knowledge within their neural weights (parametric memory). However, parametric
memory suffers from severe failure modes: models hallucinate factual claims, fail to provide precise source attributions, and cannot be
updated without expensive retraining. We address these deficiencies by coupling parametric neural generators with non-parametric external
vector memory retrieved via Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR).
2. RAG Architecture and Mathematical Formulation
RAG leverages a retriever p_eta(z|x) parameterized by BERT encoders and a generator p_theta(y_i|x, z, y_1:i-1) parameterized by BART.
Given query x, the retriever computes top-k documents z using maximum inner product search (MIPS): p_eta(z|x) proportional to exp(d(z)^T
* q(x)).
RAG-Sequence marginalizes over passages for the entire sequence: p_RAG-Seq(y|x) = sum_{z in Top-k} p_eta(z|x) * prod_{i}
p_theta(y_i|x, z, y_1:i-1).
RAG-Token marginalizes per token: p_RAG-Tok(y|x) = prod_{i} sum_{z in Top-k} p_eta(z|x) * p_theta(y_i|x, z, y_1:i-1).
Page 1

3. Training Paradigm & End-to-End Joint Optimization
The retriever and generator are trained end-to-end without direct supervision on which document should be retrieved. Minimizing negative
log-likelihood of target tokens backpropagates gradients through both the BART generator and the query document encoder, steering the
dense vector space towards documents that enhance generation accuracy.
3.1 Knowledge Update and Modularity
A defining architectural advantage of RAG is modularity: as real-world facts change, the non-parametric document index can be replaced or
hot-swapped in minutes without retraining the generative neural weights.
Page 2

4. Experimental Results on Open-Domain Benchmarks
On open-domain Question Answering (Natural Questions, WebQuestions, CuratedTREC), RAG sets state-of-the-art results, scoring 44.5%
exact match on Natural Questions, outperforming T5 11B while using only 400M parameters. On FEVER fact verification, RAG achieves
89.5% accuracy, demonstrating superior truthfulness and hallucination mitigation.
5. Core Limitations and Retrieval Bottlenecks
RAG systems have clear limitations: Retrieval errors propagate into generation?if top-k documents do not contain the target fact or contain
adversarial misinformation, the generator hallucinates. Additionally, standard single-hop retrieval cannot perform multi-step multi-hop
reasoning across disconnected documents without agentic iterative retrieval loops.
6. Future Horizons
Critical frontiers include multi-hop iterative agentic RAG, graph-augmented retrieval, and real-time streaming citation verification.
Page 3

f4f29eb1.title: Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model
f4f29eb1.author: Unknown Author
f4f29eb1.abstract: While large-scale unsupervised language models learn broad world knowledge and reasoning capabilities, steering their behavior to human preferences via Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) has become essential. Existing RLHF pipelines are complex and unstable, typically fitting a separate reward model to human preferences, then training a policy with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) while avoiding drift from the reference policy. In this paper, we show how to optimize language models directly from preferences without reinforcement learning. We introduce Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), which derives an exact closed-form mapping between the reward function and the optimal policy. DPO implicitly optimizes the same objective as RLHF under a Bradley-Terry preference model using a simple binary cross-entropy loss. Experiments show DPO matches or outperforms PPO on summarization and dialogue while eliminating training instability and hyperparameter sensitivity.

full_text_pages.text:
Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model
Authors: Rafael Rafailov, Archit Sharma, Eric Mitchell, Stefano Ermon, Christopher D. Manning, Chelsea Finn (Stanford University)
ABSTRACT
While large-scale unsupervised language models learn broad world knowledge and reasoning capabilities, steering their behavior to human
preferences via Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) has become essential. Existing RLHF pipelines are complex and
unstable, typically fitting a separate reward model to human preferences, then training a policy with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)
while avoiding drift from the reference policy. In this paper, we show how to optimize language models directly from preferences without
reinforcement learning. We introduce Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), which derives an exact closed-form mapping between the
reward function and the optimal policy. DPO implicitly optimizes the same objective as RLHF under a Bradley-Terry preference model using
a simple binary cross-entropy loss. Experiments show DPO matches or outperforms PPO on summarization and dialogue while eliminating
training instability and hyperparameter sensitivity.
1. Introduction: The Instability of RLHF with PPO
Aligning large language models with human preferences typically relies on Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). The
standard pipeline comprises three stages: (1) Supervised fine-tuning, (2) Training a distinct reward model on human pairwise preferences,
and (3) Optimizing the policy via PPO against the learned reward with a KL-divergence penalty. PPO is notoriously unstable, sensitive to
hyperparameters, and computationally demanding, requiring concurrent hosting of the actor, critic, reward, and reference models in GPU
memory.
2. Mathematical Derivation of DPO
DPO re-parameterizes the reward function r(x, y) directly in terms of the optimal policy pi_theta and reference policy pi_ref: r(x, y) = beta *
log(pi_theta(y|x) / pi_ref(y|x)) + beta * log(Z(x)).
Substituting this analytical formulation into the Bradley-Terry preference model P(y_w > y_l | x) = sigma(r(x, y_w) - r(x, y_l)) yields the exact
DPO objective:
L_DPO(pi_theta; pi_ref) = -E_{(x, y_w, y_l)} [ log sigma( beta * log(pi_theta(y_w|x) / pi_ref(y_w|x)) - beta * log(pi_theta(y_l|x) / pi_ref(y_l|x)) )
].
Page 1

3. Algorithmic Mechanics: Reward-Free Implicit Optimization
The gradient of L_DPO increases the likelihood of preferred completions y_w and decreases the likelihood of dispreferred completions y_l,
weighted by how strongly the implicit reward model misranks them. DPO completely bypasses reinforcement learning: it uses standard
supervised binary cross-entropy, requires zero sampling during training, fits within standard optimization loops, and halves GPU memory
requirements by eliminating the PPO critic and separate reward network.
3.1 Theoretical Equivalence
We prove that DPO solves the identical constrained KL-regularized reward maximization problem as traditional PPO without
approximations.
Page 2

4. Empirical Results on Summarization and Dialogue
On TL;DR summarization, DPO outperforms PPO with a win-rate of 61% over reference completions and higher temperature robustness.
On Anthropic Helpful and Harmless dialogue evaluations, DPO reaches superior Pareto frontiers of reward vs KL divergence, training in a
fraction of the wall-clock time.
5. Limitations and Distributional Assumptions
DPO relies on the Bradley-Terry pairwise preference assumption; it struggles with intransitive preferences where A > B and B > C but C >
A. Second, DPO is offline: it optimizes over fixed static preference datasets without on-policy exploration, making it vulnerable to
out-of-distribution hallucinations when evaluating completions generated far from the reference policy.
6. Future Directions
Key avenues include online iterative DPO with self-generated preference pairs, group-preference formulations, and integrating DPO with
reasoning chain-of-thought verification.
Page 3

f6570939.title: DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Lear
f6570939.author: Authors: DeepSeek-AI
f6570939.abstract: We introduce our first-generation reasoning models, DeepSeek-R1-Zero and DeepSeek-R1. DeepSeek-R1-Zero is trained via large-scale reinforcement learning (RL) directly on base models without preliminary supervised fine-tuning (SFT). We demonstrate that pure RL can incentivize sophisticated reasoning behaviors, including chain-of-thought verification, reflection, self-correction, and generating long thinking tokens before final answers. DeepSeek-R1-Zero achieves 71.0% pass@1 on AIME 2024 and 86.6% on MATH-500. To resolve language mixing and readability issues in pure RL, we develop DeepSeek-R1, which combines cold-start reasoning data with multi-stage RL. DeepSeek-R1 matches OpenAI-o1 across mathematics, coding, and logical reasoning benchmarks. Furthermore, we distill reasoning capabilities into lightweight 1.5B, 7B, 14B, and 32B models, outperforming open-source baselines.

full_text_pages.text:
DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Lear
Authors: DeepSeek-AI
ABSTRACT
We introduce our first-generation reasoning models, DeepSeek-R1-Zero and DeepSeek-R1. DeepSeek-R1-Zero is trained via large-scale
reinforcement learning (RL) directly on base models without preliminary supervised fine-tuning (SFT). We demonstrate that pure RL can
incentivize sophisticated reasoning behaviors, including chain-of-thought verification, reflection, self-correction, and generating long thinking
tokens before final answers. DeepSeek-R1-Zero achieves 71.0% pass@1 on AIME 2024 and 86.6% on MATH-500. To resolve language
mixing and readability issues in pure RL, we develop DeepSeek-R1, which combines cold-start reasoning data with multi-stage RL.
DeepSeek-R1 matches OpenAI-o1 across mathematics, coding, and logical reasoning benchmarks. Furthermore, we distill reasoning
capabilities into lightweight 1.5B, 7B, 14B, and 32B models, outperforming open-source baselines.
1. Introduction: The Emergence of Pure RL Reasoning
Traditional post-training heavily depends on supervised fine-tuning (SFT) over curated human demonstrations. We investigate whether
reasoning capabilities can emerge spontaneously through pure reinforcement learning without human demonstration data. Using Group
Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), we train base language models using rule-based reward signals on mathematical and code
benchmarks. Without any SFT examples, DeepSeek-R1-Zero spontaneously learns to generate extensive thinking traces, reconsider initial
assumptions, and execute runtime self-correction.
2. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) Algorithm
Instead of training a critic network of equal size to the policy (as in PPO), GRPO samples a group of G candidate outputs {o_1, o_2, ...,
o_G} for query q from the old policy pi_theta_old. The reward r_i is computed using rule-based verifiers (compiler execution correctness for
code, numerical equivalence for math). The advantage A_i is normalized across the group: A_i = (r_i - mean(r)) / std(r). This saves
enormous memory and eliminates the value network entirely.
Page 1

3. The DeepSeek-R1 Multi-Stage Training Pipeline
To address language inconsistency and unstructured output in R1-Zero, DeepSeek-R1 adopts a four-stage pipeline:
Stage 1: Cold-start SFT with several thousand high-quality human-readable long chain-of-thought examples.
Stage 2: Reasoning-oriented RL using GRPO on math, logic, and coding benchmarks.
Stage 3: Rejection sampling to generate 800k synthetic reasoning and general-domain examples for comprehensive SFT.
Stage 4: Secondary RL with combined rule-based accuracy rewards and human preference alignment rewards.
3.1 Knowledge Distillation into Dense Architectures
We distill reasoning tokens from DeepSeek-R1 into smaller dense Qwen and Llama architectures (1.5B, 7B, 14B, 32B). Distillation yields
superior results compared to training small models with RL from scratch.
Page 2

4. Benchmark Performance & Mathematical Breakthroughs
DeepSeek-R1 records 79.8% pass@1 on AIME 2024 (matching OpenAI-o1-1217), 97.3% on MATH-500, and 2029 Elo on Codeforces (top
96.3th percentile). The distilled 32B model attains 72.6% on AIME 2024, surpassing all open-source models of comparable scale.
5. Limitations and Reasoning Vulnerabilities
DeepSeek-R1 possesses clear limitations: First, inference latency is high due to long thinking traces (often several thousand reasoning
tokens per query). Second, while strong in verifiable STEM domains with rule-based ground-truth rewards, applying GRPO to creative
writing or subjective policy tasks remains challenging due to lack of deterministic reward verifiers. Third, overthinking on simple factual
queries can lead to unnecessary computational overhead.
6. Future Research Trajectories
Key frontiers include dynamic thinking token budget allocation, extending pure RL reasoning to multi-modal visual proofs, and eliminating
reasoning token verbosity through length penalties.
Page 3

full_text_pages.text:
LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models
Authors: Hugo Touvron, Thibaut Lavril, Gautier Izacard, Xavier Martinet, Marie-Anne Lachaux, Timothée Lacroix, Baptiste Rozière, Naman Goyal
ABSTRACT
We introduce LLaMA, a collection of foundation language models ranging from 7B to 65B parameters. We train our models on trillions of
tokens, and show that it is possible to train state-of-the-art models using publicly available datasets exclusively, without resorting to
proprietary and inaccessible datasets. In particular, LLaMA-13B outperforms GPT-3 (175B) on most benchmarks, and LLaMA-65B is
competitive with the best models, Chinchilla-70B and PaLM-540B. Unlike previous efforts which optimized for training FLOPs alone, our
focus is on serving efficiency: a smaller model trained on more data is cheaper to run at inference time.
1. Introduction & The Inference Efficiency Imperative
Most recent work on large language models has focused on scaling parameter counts to hundreds of billions. However, recent scaling laws
(Hoffmann et al., 2022) indicate that for a given compute budget, smaller models trained on significantly more data achieve superior
downstream performance. Crucially, when considering total lifecycle cost, inference latency and hardware requirements dominate. We train
models ranging from 7B to 65B parameters on 1.0T to 1.4T tokens of publicly accessible text.
2. Architectural Modernizations
LLaMA incorporates three key improvements over the standard Transformer:
1. Pre-normalization (RMSNorm): Normalize input of each transformer sub-layer using RMSNorm to improve training stability.
2. SwiGLU Activation Function: Replace ReLU non-linearity with SwiGLU activation (with dimension 2/3 * 4d) to boost model expressivity.
3. Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE): Employ rotary embeddings at each layer to improve relative position modeling and extrapolation.
Page 1

3. Pre-training Data Pipeline & Tokenizer
The training corpus comprises 1.4 trillion tokens drawn exclusively from public sources: CommonCrawl (67%), C4 (15%), GitHub (4.5%),
Wikipedia (4.5%), Gutenberg & Books3 (4.5%), ArXiv (2.5%), and Stack Exchange (2.0%). We utilize a Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) tokenizer
with 32,000 tokens, treating all numbers as individual digits to avoid arithmetic tokenization fragmentation.
Page 2

4. Benchmark Performance Across Tasks
On common-sense reasoning benchmarks (BoolQ, PIQA, SIQA, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC), LLaMA-13B surpasses GPT-3 (175B)
despite being over 10x smaller. On MMLU, LLaMA-65B achieves 63.4%, trailing only Chinchilla-70B (67.5%) and PaLM 540B (69.3%). On
GSM8K grade-school math, LLaMA-65B records 50.9%.
5. Limitations and Social Impact Disclosures
LLaMA models exhibit standard autoregressive vulnerabilities: propensity to generate hallucinations, potential toxicity generation without
safety RLHF alignment, and linguistic over-representation of English (82% of pre-training tokens). Additionally, models were released as
base weights without fine-tuned instruction following.
6. Future Directions
Open priorities include scaling token horizons beyond 2T tokens, fine-grained instruction alignment (Llama-2/3), and extending native
context window lengths beyond 2048 tokens.
Page 3

full_text_pages.text:
Hybrid State Space Models for Long Sequences
Authors: ResearchMind Academic Team
ABSTRACT
An empirical study evaluating selective state space models against quadratic attention mechanisms.
1. Introduction & Research Objectives
This research investigates Hybrid State Space Models for Long Sequences. The primary research objective is to advance state-of-the-art
methodology in machine learning, offering theoretical justifications and empirical validation across standard benchmarks.
Page 1

2. Methodology & Proposed Architecture
Hardware-aware selective scan kernels with SRAM cache tiling.
3. Empirical Results & Comparative Evaluation
Achieves linear compute complexity O(N) with 4.5x faster generation throughput.
Page 2

4. Disclosed Limitations & Boundary Conditions
Lack of associative memory on multi-hop associative recall tasks.
5. Future Research Directions & Open Inquiries
Future trajectories focus on sub-quadratic attention scaling, automated hyperparameter optimization, and extending the methodology to
multi-modal visual and auditory reasoning.
